thread.title: Facebook reportedly pays users to install app that harvests their phone data - MarketWatch

author: Mike Murphy
title: Facebook reportedly pays users to install app that harvests their phone data - MarketWatch
text:
For the past three years, Facebook Inc. secretly paid users for installing an app that harvests all their phone and web activity, according to a new report. Apple has since revoked the company’s access.
TechCrunch on Tuesday reported that since 2016, Facebook FB, +3.56% paid users between the ages of 13 and 35 up to $20 a month if they install a “Facebook Research” mobile app that gives the company root access to their devices — and apparently the ability to access virtually all data, including emails, private messages, web searches, browsing history and location tracking.
Security expert Will Strafach told TechCrunch the app is “appalling.” “This hands Facebook continuous access to the most sensitive data about you,” he said.
The breadth of the app’s data harvesting was in violation of Apple Inc.’s AAPL, +5.29% iOS platform rules. The smartphone maker revoked Facebook’s “Enterprise Certificate,” which gave the company the ability to distribute apps without going through the App Store. The revocation affected not just Facebook’s Research app, but also other internal tools used for beta testing features and learning about company transportation options.
Don’t miss: Apple revenue should continue to shrink, so why is the stock up?
Last year, Facebook was forced to remove its Onavo data-security app from Apple’s app store because it violated Apple’s data-collection policies.
Apple Chief Executive Tim Cook has been critical of Facebook’s data-collection practices in the past. The company is also dealing with an app-related public-relations crisis of its own, after it was revealed that a FaceTime bug inadvertently allowed users to spy on the cameras and microphones of users who hadn’t yet picked up a call.
Facebook has weathered a series of data-related scandals in recent years — including one involving Cambridge Analytica’s data mining — and its shares have tumbled 22% over the past 12 months, but Facebook is still expected to post the most profitable quarter in its history on Wednesday.
